title: Data Visualization Tools Market
note: Background for the thesis introduction, not a research paper. The publisher updates the market figures over time.

title: Trio: A System for Data, Uncertainty, and Lineage
citation: Parag Agrawal, Omar Benjelloun, Anish Das Sarma, Chris Hayworth, Shubha Nabar, Tomoe Sugihara and Jennifer Widom · VLDB 2006
note: Trio keeps uncertain values and their lineage together, so an answer can carry both its confidence and its derivation. The thesis lists this demo’s authors under the title of reference [9].

title: GProM: A Swiss Army Knife for Your Provenance Needs
citation: Bahareh Arab, Su Feng, Boris Glavic, Seokki Lee, Xing Niu and Qitian Zeng · IEEE Data Engineering Bulletin 2018
note: GProM rewrites a request for provenance into a query the underlying database can execute. This puts lineage support in middleware rather than inside each database engine.

title: Column-Stores vs. Row-Stores: How Different Are They Really?
citation: Daniel J. Abadi, Samuel R. Madden and Nabil Hachem · SIGMOD 2008
note: Storing columns separately is only part of the story. The experiments isolate execution techniques, including delaying the reconstruction of full rows.

title: Provenance for Interactive Visualizations
citation: Fotis Psallidas and Eugene Wu · HILDA 2018
note: Click a mark in a chart and ask which records produced it. The paper shows how to express interactions like this as provenance queries.

title: Perm: Processing Provenance and Data on the Same Data Model through Query Rewriting
citation: Boris Glavic and Gustavo Alonso · ICDE 2009
note: Perm rewrites a relational query to return provenance alongside data. The result is relational too, so another SQL query can inspect it.

title: Smoked Duck
citation: Cited as unpublished in the thesis · link to the project repository
note: This is the project my thesis extended. It records which input rows contribute to each output while DuckDB’s operators run.

title: PUG: A Framework and Practical Implementation for Why and Why-Not Provenance
citation: Seokki Lee, Bertram Ludäscher and Boris Glavic · The VLDB Journal 2019
note: PUG explains missing answers as well as returned ones. It builds a graph of the facts and rule applications relevant to the question. The arXiv link is the extended version.

title: An Introduction to ULDBs and the Trio System
citation: Omar Benjelloun, Anish Das Sarma, Chris Hayworth and Jennifer Widom · Stanford InfoLab / IEEE Data Engineering Bulletin 2006
note: The uncertainty-lineage database model links alternative values to their derivations. TriQL extends SQL so a query can ask about lineage and confidence.

title: Smoke: Fine-grained Lineage at Interactive Speed
citation: Fotis Psallidas and Eugene Wu · VLDB 2018
note: If someone clicks a chart to inspect a result, rerunning the original query can be too slow. Smoke shows how recording row relationships during execution can make that later interaction fast.

title: DuckDB: an Embeddable Analytical Database
citation: Mark Raasveldt and Hannes Mühleisen · SIGMOD 2019
note: Analytical queries don't require a separate database server. DuckDB brings a vectorized engine into the application process, the same execution model my thesis extended to answer lineage queries.

title: Provenance Semirings
citation: Todd J. Green, Grigoris Karvounarakis and Val Tannen · PODS 2007
note: Annotate each input tuple with a symbol. Multiplication records inputs used together; addition records alternative derivations of the same result.

title: You Say ‘What’, I Hear ‘Where’ and ‘Why’: (Mis-)Interpreting SQL to Derive Fine-Grained Provenance
citation: Tobias Müller, Benjamin Dietrich and Torsten Grust · PVLDB 2018
note: One query execution records control decisions. A second follows that record to compute dependencies rather than values, revealing where results came from and why they appeared.

title: Tracing the Lineage of View Data in a Warehousing Environment
citation: Yingwei Cui, Jennifer Widom and Janet L. Wiener · ACM Transactions on Database Systems 2000
note: Given a tuple in a warehouse view, which source tuples contributed to it? The paper studies how to trace those inputs through relational view definitions.
